1 
Innovaccer, Inc. 
201 Mission Street, Ste. 2900 
San Francisco, CA 94105 
June 15, 2026 
The Honorable Mehmet Oz, MD 
Administrator, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, MD 21244-1850 
Submitted electronically via Regulations.gov 
Re: CMS-0062-P, RIN 0938-AV44 - Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection 
and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs 
Dear Administrator Oz, 
Innovaccer, Inc. (Innovaccer) submits these comments on the Interoperability Standards and 
Prior Authorization for Drugs proposed rule. Innovaccer is an enterprise AI and data platform 
that acts as the healthcare context layer for health systems, providers, accountable care 
organizations, payers, health plans, and public sector agencies. Gravity, the autonomous 
healthcare platform, integrates with more than 100 electronic health record and operational 
systems and turns the fragmented information those systems hold into high-quality, 
standardized data that powers agentic automation across population health, care management, 
quality, revenue cycle, prior authorization, and patient access. 
That work gives us a direct view of where prior authorization breaks and what fixes it. Our Flow 
platform automates prior authorization, referrals, coding, and denials for providers. Our LRx360 
specialty pharmacy platform, co-developed with Longitude Rx, verifies benefits and starts prior 
authorization before the drug reaches the pharmacy. Pharmacy Quality Solutions by Innovaccer 
operates the EQUIPP platform to enable value based contracting efforts between healthcare 
payers and the majority of community pharmacies in the United States. Across these, the same 
lesson holds: prior authorization stalls because the clinical record sits in one system, payer 
policy in another, and the transaction in a third, and because the standards meant to connect 
them are recommended rather than required. This rule addresses that directly, and we support 
its direction. 
We organize our comments around the provisions where we have the most direct experience. In 
short: 
Required beats recommended. Moving the Da Vinci FHIR implementation guides from 
recommended to required, and adopting FHIR as a HIPAA standard, removes the optionality 
that allows dominant vendors to stall on meaningful implementation. 
Extend prior authorization to drugs, coherently. The pharmacy-benefit and medical-benefit 
tracks must be kept aligned so that providers and platforms do not have to build and maintain 
 
2 
two disconnected pipelines, an outcome that would recreate the fragmentation this rule is 
designed to eliminate. 
Make compliance verifiable. Endpoint reporting, usage-metrics reporting, conformance 
testing, and a public test sandbox are the difference between a published API and a usable one. 
Without them, nominal compliance becomes a ceiling rather than a floor. 
Sequence the standards realistically. Require versions only once they are stable and provide 
a clear transition path where FHIR and the legacy X12 278 transaction coexist. The burden 
should fall on standardization, not on duplicate work. 
Our detailed comments follow. 
1. Adopt the FHIR implementation guides as requirements, not recommendations 
Innovaccer supports moving the Health Level Seven (HL7) FHIR Da Vinci implementation 
guides, including Coverage Requirements Discovery (CRD), Documentation Templates and 
Rules (DTR), and Prior Authorization Support (PAS), from recommended to required for the 
interoperability application programming interfaces (APIs), and adopting updated versions in 45 
CFR 170.215. Recommendation has not been enough. When each payer is free to implement a 
different subset of these guides, or none, automation degrades to portals, fax, and one-off 
integrations, and the providers and platforms acting on a patient's behalf absorb the cost. 
We support the flexibility to use any unexpired version of a standard, with two requests. First, 
CMS should require a version only after it is balloted and stable, with enough lead time before 
the compliance date so that payers and connecting parties implement against a fixed target. 
Second, CMS should set a sunset window for superseded versions, so that the unexpired-
version flexibility does not allow a payer to remain on the oldest version indefinitely and 
undercut the consistency the requirement is meant to create. 
2. Extend electronic prior authorization to drugs, and keep the two benefit tracks 
coherent 
Innovaccer supports requiring electronic prior authorization for drugs: the National Council for 
Prescription Drug Programs (NCPDP) standards, including SCRIPT, for drugs covered under 
the pharmacy benefit, and the FHIR-based Prior Authorization API for drugs covered under the 
medical benefit. We also support requiring the NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit and 
Formulary and Benefit standards as complements. Real-time benefit and formulary visibility at 
the moment of prescribing is where avoidable delay is removed, and it is the foundation of 
faster, more reliable time to therapy. 
As a practical matter, platforms that serve both benefits will build to the NCPDP standards 
regardless, so our point here is about reducing duplicated work rather than a condition on the 
proposal. A single drug can move between the pharmacy and medical benefits, and a single 
provider organization commonly handles both. Where the NCPDP path and the FHIR PAS path 
share data elements and decision semantics, information moves between them without re-entry, 
and providers and platforms avoid maintaining two disconnected pipelines for what is, to the 
patient, one decision. We encourage CMS to align the two tracks to that end. 
 
3 
Our pharmacy experience points to one addition. The proposed rule describes the Real-Time 
Prescription Benefit and Formulary and Benefit standards as serving providers at the point of 
prescribing. In practice, this benefit, coverage, and prior-authorization information is surfaced to 
prescribers in provider portals and to members in member-facing apps, but typically not to the 
pharmacy. Pharmacists are often the first to encounter a coverage or prior-authorization 
problem when a patient arrives to pick up a drug. We encourage CMS to ensure that the same 
real-time benefit, formulary, and status information is made available to pharmacies, so the 
pharmacy can help the patient directly rather than sending them back to the prescriber. This 
matters most for community pharmacies, which serve patients who may have no other 
immediate point of contact with the care team. 
Relatedly, prior-authorization status is often visible only through proprietary vendor networks 
rather than through open, standardized channels. When a request stalls or falls outside the 
normal automated path, the parties who need its status, including the pharmacy, may have no 
standards-based way to see it. Consistent with our broader position that openly specified 
standards should carry interoperable exchange, we encourage CMS to ensure that prior-
authorization status can be conveyed through the open standards adopted in this rule and is not 
confined to any single proprietary platform. 
On the proposed exception for qualified health plan (QHP) issuers on the Federally-facilitated 
Exchanges (FFEs) from the pharmacy-benefit requirement, we ask CMS to keep it narrow and 
time-limited. A standing opt-out would reintroduce, for a class of plans, the variability the rule is 
trying to remove. 
3. Shorten decision timeframes and require a structured reason for denial 
Innovaccer supports shortening and aligning prior-authorization decision timeframes for drugs 
across programs, and extending the framework to QHP issuers on the FFEs that were 
previously outside it. Shorter clocks make the manual scramble to assemble a request inside a 
tight window untenable, which is precisely the work that automation should carry. 
We strongly support requiring payers to give the provider a specific reason for any drug prior-
authorization denial, and we ask CMS to require that reason as a structured, coded field in the 
FHIR PAS response rather than as free text. A coded denial reason can be acted on 
automatically: it lets a provider's systems respond, resubmit with the missing element, or appeal 
without a person first reading and interpreting a letter. A free-text reason preserves the very 
manual step the rule is trying to remove. Structured denial reasons also let payers and providers 
see patterns across decisions and improve how the next request is prepared. 
These shorter timeframes are workable only if the required FHIR APIs are in place. A payer 
cannot reliably decide within a 24-hour or 72-hour window while a provider still assembles and 
submits requests through portals and fax. This reinforces the case for requiring the 
implementation guides in section II.A rather than recommending them; the timeframe and the 
standard depend on each other. 
4. Make compliance verifiable: endpoint reporting, usage metrics, conformance 
testing, and a sandbox 
 
4 
A standard that is published but not usable does not move data. Innovaccer connects to payer 
APIs every day, and the difference between an API that exists on paper and one that works in 
production is the central practical problem in interoperability today. We therefore strongly 
support CMS's proposals requiring impacted payers to report their API endpoints for publication 
and to report usage metrics across the Patient Access, Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer, and 
Prior Authorization APIs. A CMS-published, machine-readable directory of payer FHIR 
endpoints, kept current, is the practical precondition for any third party to connect at all; today, 
finding and onboarding to a payer's FHIR endpoint is a manual hunt that adds cost before a 
single transaction has occurred.  
 
Usage metrics address the next problem: whether an API is actually used or merely published. 
We suggest CMS strengthen those metrics by including a measure of third-party connection 
success or error rates alongside call volume, since volume alone does not distinguish a 
functioning API from one that rejects connections in practice. On the prior-authorization metrics, 
we support adding numeric counts alongside the existing percentage metrics and the new 
denial and appeal measures; numeric counts and consistent definitions are what make payer 
behavior comparable across plans. We also support requiring public posting of drug prior-
authorization metrics for the same reason.  
Taken together, endpoint reporting, usage metrics, and expanded PA metrics are the 
transparency layer that keeps compliance honest and we therefore support, together, the 
reporting provisions in this rule and the implementation ideas raised in the related request for 
information. 
5. Adopt FHIR PAS as a HIPAA standard for the prior-authorization transaction 
Innovaccer strongly supports the proposal to adopt the HL7 FHIR Da Vinci PAS implementation 
guide as a HIPAA standard for the referral certification and authorization transaction and the 
associated eligibility transactions, applying to all HIPAA covered entities rather than only to 
impacted payers. This is the most consequential standards step in the rule. A HIPAA-level FHIR 
standard is what makes prior-authorization automation portable across every payer and 
provider, not just the plans CMS regulates directly, and it is consistent with our long-held 
position that openly specified standards, rather than proprietary pathways controlled by 
individual vendors, should carry interoperable exchange. 
We ask CMS and HHS to manage the transition deliberately. For a period, FHIR PAS and the 
legacy X12 278 transaction will necessarily coexist, since the industry cannot move to a new 
standard all at once. CMS should make that period well-defined and as short as is reasonable, 
and publish a clear timeline and transition path, so that providers, clearinghouses, and 
intermediaries move toward the FHIR standard rather than maintaining two transaction pipelines 
indefinitely. Conformance expectations should apply to clearinghouses and other intermediaries 
as well, so the standard is not weakened at the points where transactions are handed off. 
 
 
 
5 
6. Request for Information (RFI): Extend event notifications for care coordination 
On the RFI about electronic event notifications for value-based care and care coordination, 
Innovaccer's central recommendation is to expand who receives notifications rather than to 
mandate a new underlying technology. The clearest gain is extending notifications beyond 
hospitals and recognizing accountable care organizations and pharmacies of all types, including 
community pharmacies, as recipients. Real-time admission, discharge, and transfer (ADT) 
signals are the trigger for timely care management and for pharmacy-based interventions that 
protect medication adherence and patient safety, and the participants who can act on them are 
broader than the current notification requirements reach. 
We would caution against requiring a new FHIR-based notification technology as the means to 
that end. FHIR-based messaging is not yet widely adopted for this use, and standing up a 
generalized notification ecosystem on it would require many participants, including those with 
limited resources, to start from scratch, which would slow the very expansion the rule is trying to 
achieve. The existing ADT exchange ecosystem, while imperfect, already supports a wide range 
of participants and can extend to new recipients comparatively quickly. We recommend CMS 
prioritize broadening the audience over replacing the transport. Innovaccer operates event 
notification and care coordination across more than 100 systems, and PQS by Innovaccer 
reaches the large majority of community pharmacies in the country; we would welcome the 
chance to share what makes these notifications actionable in practice. 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this proposed rule. Innovaccer supports CMS in 
moving from recommended standards to required, verifiable ones, and our team is available to 
discuss any of these comments in more detail. 
Sincerely, 
Abhinav Shashank 
CEO and Co-Founder, Innovaccer 
Dave Cassel, MS 
Senior Vice President, Interoperability 
Todd Sega, Pharm.D, MBA 
Managing Director of Pharmacy 
Lisa Bari, MBA, MPH 
Vice President, Policy and Partnerships

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Innovaccer, Inc.; signed by Abhinav Shashank, Dave Cassel, Todd Sega, and Lisa Bari.
- **Stakeholder type:** Technology Vendor
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Enterprise AI and data platform serving health systems, providers, ACOs, payers, health plans, and public sector agencies. Innovaccer references its Gravity platform, Flow prior authorization automation platform, LRx360 specialty pharmacy platform, and Pharmacy Quality Solutions/EQUIPP platform serving community pharmacies.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Innovaccer strongly supports CMS' direction, especially moving Da Vinci FHIR IGs from recommended to required and adopting FHIR PAS as a HIPAA prior authorization standard. It asks CMS to align pharmacy- and medical-benefit tracks, require structured denial reasons, make compliance verifiable through endpoint reporting/usage metrics/conformance testing/sandboxes, manage version transitions realistically, and broaden ADT/event notification recipients without mandating a new FHIR notification transport.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS; GENERAL/RFI event notifications.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** 45 CFR 170.215; CMS-0062-P; RIN 0938-AV44.
- **Standards referenced:** HL7 FHIR, Da Vinci CRD, DTR, PAS, NCPDP SCRIPT, NCPDP RTPB, NCPDP Formulary & Benefit, X12 278, ADT event notifications.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Required FHIR implementation guides**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Optional standards allow payer and vendor variation, leading to portals, fax, one-off integrations, and provider/platform burden.
- **Specific request:** Require HL7 FHIR Da Vinci CRD, DTR, and PAS implementation guides for interoperability APIs and adopt updated versions in 45 CFR 170.215.

**Topic 2: Version stability and sunset windows**
- **Provision ID:** ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE / FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Unexpired-version flexibility supports implementation but may allow payers to remain indefinitely on older versions, undermining consistency.
- **Specific request:** Require versions only after they are balloted and stable, provide sufficient lead time, and establish sunset windows for superseded versions.

**Topic 3: Coherent medical- and pharmacy-benefit drug PA tracks**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL / PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support with modification
- **Rationale:** A single drug can move between pharmacy and medical benefits, and provider organizations often handle both. Separate pipelines would recreate fragmentation and duplicate work.
- **Specific request:** Align shared data elements and decision semantics between NCPDP and FHIR PAS tracks so information can move without re-entry.

**Topic 4: Pharmacy access to RTPB/F&B/status information**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Pharmacists are often the first to encounter coverage or PA problems when a patient arrives to pick up a drug, yet real-time benefit/formulary/status data is often surfaced to prescribers or members but not pharmacies.
- **Specific request:** Ensure pharmacies, especially community pharmacies, can access real-time benefit, formulary, and PA status information.

**Topic 5: QHP pharmacy-benefit exception**
- **Provision ID:** FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS / PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** A broad or permanent QHP issuer opt-out would reintroduce variability.
- **Specific request:** Keep any QHP issuer exception from pharmacy-benefit requirements narrow and time-limited.

**Topic 6: Decision timeframes and structured denial reasons**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS / PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support with modification
- **Rationale:** Shorter clocks increase the need for automated standards-based workflows. Free-text denial reasons preserve manual work and are harder to act on.
- **Specific request:** Shorten and align drug PA timeframes, require payers to provide specific denial reasons as structured coded fields in FHIR PAS responses, and ensure denial patterns can be analyzed.

**Topic 7: Verifiable compliance**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING / API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support with modification
- **Rationale:** A published API may still be unusable in production. Metrics and endpoint directories help determine whether APIs are discoverable and actually usable.
- **Specific request:** Require a CMS-published machine-readable directory of payer FHIR endpoints, usage metrics, third-party connection success/error rates, numeric counts in PA metrics, conformance testing, and a public test sandbox.

**Topic 8: HIPAA FHIR PAS standard**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** HIPAA-level FHIR PAS adoption would make ePA portable across all covered entities, not just CMS-impacted payers, and would reduce reliance on proprietary pathways.
- **Specific request:** Adopt HL7 FHIR Da Vinci PAS as a HIPAA standard for referral certification and authorization and associated eligibility transactions, with a deliberate transition from X12 278.

**Topic 9: X12 278 coexistence and intermediary conformance**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** The industry cannot move to a new standard all at once, and dual pipelines should not persist indefinitely.
- **Specific request:** Define a clear, short transition path where FHIR PAS and X12 278 coexist; apply conformance expectations to clearinghouses and intermediaries.

**Topic 10: Event notification RFI**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** The immediate gain is expanding recipients of existing notifications, while mandating new FHIR-based notification technology could slow implementation because FHIR messaging is not yet widely adopted for this use.
- **Specific request:** Extend ADT notifications to ACOs and pharmacies, including community pharmacies, using existing ADT exchange infrastructure rather than mandating new FHIR transport.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1:** Strongly supports requiring rather than recommending Da Vinci CRD, DTR, and PAS IGs.
- **S2/S3:** Supports unexpired version flexibility only with stable, balloted versions, enough lead time, and sunset windows for older versions.
- **S12:** Supports medical-benefit drug PA via FHIR and highlights need to avoid fragmented pipelines.
- **S14:** Supports pharmacy-benefit ePA using NCPDP standards, including SCRIPT, RTPB, and F&B.
- **S15:** Responds by asking CMS to align the pharmacy- and medical-benefit tracks because drugs and provider workflows can cross benefit categories.
- **S16/S17:** Strongly supports specific denial reasons and requests structured, coded denial reasons in the FHIR PAS response.
- **S20/S43:** Supports shorter and aligned drug PA decision timeframes, but states they depend on required FHIR APIs.
- **S23/S24/S26/S27/S33:** Supports endpoint reporting and asks for a CMS-published machine-readable endpoint directory kept current.
- **S29/S30/S34/S35:** Supports usage metrics and public posting; recommends adding connection success/error rates and numeric counts.
- **S31:** Requests any QHP issuer exception from pharmacy-benefit requirements be narrow and time-limited.
- **S44/S45/S46/S47/S53/S54/S55:** Supports FHIR PAS as a HIPAA standard across covered entities, with defined coexistence with X12 278, clear timelines, conformance expectations, and testing.
- **S60/S63:** Addresses versioning through stable-version requirements and sunset windows.
- **S66-S82:** Responds to event notification RFI by supporting expanded ADT recipients while cautioning against mandating new FHIR notification technology.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Require HL7 FHIR Da Vinci CRD, DTR, and PAS IGs instead of leaving them recommended.
2. Adopt updated versions in 45 CFR 170.215 only after ballot stability and adequate lead time.
3. Establish sunset windows for superseded versions.
4. Require NCPDP standards for pharmacy-benefit drug ePA and FHIR Prior Authorization API for medical-benefit drugs.
5. Align data elements and decision semantics across NCPDP and FHIR PAS workflows.
6. Make real-time benefit, formulary, and PA status information available to pharmacies.
7. Require PA status exchange through open standards rather than proprietary networks alone.
8. Keep any QHP pharmacy-benefit exception narrow and time-limited.
9. Require structured, coded denial reasons in FHIR PAS responses.
10. Require endpoint reporting, usage metrics, conformance testing, and a public test sandbox.
11. Include third-party connection success/error rates and numeric PA counts in reported metrics.
12. Adopt FHIR PAS as a HIPAA PA standard and define a clear transition from X12 278.
13. Apply conformance expectations to clearinghouses and intermediaries.
14. Expand ADT recipients to ACOs and pharmacies without mandating new FHIR notification technology.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Optional standards, disconnected medical/pharmacy benefit pipelines, opaque proprietary PA status channels, free-text denial reasons, nominal API compliance, indefinite dual FHIR/X12 pipelines, and over-prescriptive FHIR event notification requirements.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Continued fax/portal workflows, duplicate provider/platform work, delayed time to therapy, pharmacies unable to help patients at pickup, unusable APIs, and prolonged maintenance of two transaction pipelines.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Fragmented clinical records/payer policy/transactions, optional IG implementation, lack of pharmacy visibility into PA status, proprietary networks, and limited adoption of FHIR-based messaging for ADT.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** Innovaccer states Gravity integrates with more than 100 EHR and operational systems and that PQS reaches the large majority of community pharmacies.
- **Studies or research referenced:** No external studies cited.
- **Examples provided:** Provider portals, fax, one-off integrations, pharmacies encountering coverage issues at pickup, published APIs that are not usable in production, and existing ADT exchange infrastructure.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Providers, health systems, payers, health plans, ACOs, pharmacies, community pharmacies, patients, technology vendors, clearinghouses, and intermediaries.
- **Economic implications:** Standardization would reduce duplicate implementation and manual work; conformance testing and endpoint directories could lower onboarding cost.
- **Technical feasibility:** Strong support for required standards, but with stable versions, transition planning, and testing/sandbox infrastructure.
- **Patient care impact:** Positive if standards reduce delays, give pharmacies actionable information, and accelerate time to therapy.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Strongly supportive with targeted modifications
- **Tone:** Technical, assertive, implementation-focused
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Required beats recommended." - Context: Summary of why Da Vinci FHIR IGs should become mandatory.
2. "A standard that is published but not usable does not move data." - Context: Argument for endpoint reporting, usage metrics, conformance testing, and a sandbox.
3. "A coded denial reason can be acted on automatically." - Context: Request for structured denial reasons in FHIR PAS responses.
4. "A HIPAA-level FHIR standard is what makes prior-authorization automation portable across every payer and provider." - Context: Support for FHIR PAS as a HIPAA standard.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Requests deliberate sequencing, transition planning, and stable versions before requirements.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Focuses on replacing portals, fax, duplicate work, and free-text denial interpretation.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Emphasizes conformance testing, public sandbox, endpoint discovery, and standards version stability.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Requests stable balloted versions and sunset windows; warns FHIR event notification transport is not yet broadly adopted.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Frames real-time benefit/formulary visibility and automated PA as foundations for faster time to therapy.
- [x] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - Strongly supports HIPAA-level adoption of FHIR PAS across all covered entities.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Addresses providers, pharmacies, ACOs, payers, clearinghouses, and intermediaries.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Strong focus on aligning pharmacy and medical benefit PA tracks.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Supports public endpoint directories, metrics, numeric counts, and open PA status channels.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Recommends defined coexistence with X12 278 and using existing ADT exchange rather than mandating new FHIR notification transport.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Addresses dominant vendors, proprietary networks, and platform implementation realities.
